stimulus.text:
“Among the numerous advantages promised by a well constructed Union, none deserves to be more accurately developed than its tendency to break and control the violence of faction. . . . By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community. . . . Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens.”

—Publius (James Madison), Federalist No. 10, New York Daily Advertiser, November 22, 1787

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

stem: Why does Madison argue that extending the sphere of the republic helps control faction?

options.text: More interests in a larger republic stop one majority forming
A larger republic lets the strongest faction rule without opposition
options.misconception: Madison wants to stop a faction from ruling, not to hand it power; a larger sphere blocks it, not crowns it.

options.text: A larger republic removes the causes of faction from human nature
options.misconception: Madison says the causes of faction are sown in human nature and cannot be removed; only their effects can be controlled.

options.text: A larger republic lets the president overrule any faction in Congress
options.misconception: The passage never gives the president power over factions; the cure is the variety of interests itself.

rationales.A: Madison's chain is in the passage: extend the sphere, take in a greater variety of parties and interests, and it becomes less probable that a majority will share one motive to invade the rights of others.
rationales.B: Madison's cure blocks a dominant faction; it does not hand the strongest faction power.
rationales.C: Background: Madison holds the causes of faction cannot be removed, so the extended republic controls their effects, not their causes.
rationales.D: No president appears in the passage; the cure is the variety of parties and interests.
rationales.general:
1. Madison's first move: extend the sphere of the republic.
2. A wider sphere takes in a greater variety of parties and interests.
3. With more interests in play, one majority is less likely to share a single motive against others' rights.
4. Background: this is the extended-republic argument, the opposite of the old idea that republics must stay small.
Remember: more interests in the room means no one interest can fill it.
